vignette:
Patient: Mrs. A., age 70, South Asian female, divorced, professional photographer.

Mrs. A. presents with a composed, almost regal bearing that softens only when she speaks of her work. She arrives for her sessions directly from her darkroom, the faint, sharp scent of fixer clinging to her floral kurtas. She speaks of her photography with a quiet, fierce pride, describing how she has spent the last forty years capturing the weddings, the first birthdays, the naming ceremonies of her community. "I give them their memories," she says, her voice steady. "I make the joy last."

The joy, for her, did not last.

The story she tells is not of a single event, but of a long, slow poison. She was the eldest daughter in a traditional South Asian household in Nairobi, raised by a mother who was perpetually exhausted and a father who was a distant, stern provider. The primary architect of her childhood was her paternal grandmother, a woman Mrs. A. describes as "a statue of duty." This grandmother was responsible for discipline. And discipline, for Mrs. A., meant the thin, flexible cane from a neem tree.

She recalls it not with tears, but with a chilling exactness. The precise sound it made as it cut through the air. The specific, silent way her grandmother would remove her bangles and roll up her sleeve. The rule was absolute: any sign of childish will-speaking out of turn, a messy room, a bad grade-was met with a punishment that was methodical, silent, and private. The beatings were never for the transgression itself, but for the "shame" of having the transgression be seen. The goal was invisibility. "I learned to be a ghost in my own house," she whispers. "If I was good, I was not seen. If I was bad, I was seen, but only through the pain."

She escaped into a marriage at nineteen, a transaction between families that she thought was a rescue. It was not. Her husband was not physically violent, but his contempt was its own kind of cane. He belittled her photography as a "hobby," a frivolous distraction from her duties. She took the camera her brother had given her and began to shoot the world outside her window-the play of light on a wet leaf, the geometry of a shadow on a wall. It was the only time she felt solid, present. She divorced him at forty, a scandal that severed her from her family for years. She has not spoken to her grandmother since her wedding day.

Now, at seventy, the ghost has returned. The symptoms began to crystallize two years ago, after her granddaughter, Mira, was born. Mrs. A. was asked to photograph the naming ceremony. She held the camera, looked through the viewfinder at the tiny, perfect face, and froze. Her hands began to shake. She saw, for a split second, not Mira, but her own infant self, utterly defenseless. She could not press the shutter. She made an excuse about a faulty lens and left.

Since then, her world has shrunk. She can no longer photograph children. The sight of a mother gently scolding a toddler in a grocery store sends a jolt of electricity through her chest. She avoids family gatherings, terrified that the sound of a stern voice will trigger a full-body flashback where she is seven years old again, waiting for the neem cane. She has nightmares, not of the beatings themselves, but of the silent, waiting stillness that preceded them. She wakes up sweating, her limbs rigid, her mouth clamped shut, as if making a sound would be a fatal error.

Her hypervigilance is a constant companion. She scans every room for exits, for the posture of authority. She has become a master of preemptive avoidance, canceling jobs weeks in advance if the client's tone on the phone is too firm. Her PCL-5 score of 75 reflects a life held in a state of siege by a past that is not a memory, but a present tense reality. She is not an old woman remembering a difficult childhood. She is a terrified little girl, hiding in the body of a celebrated artist, waiting for the silence to break.
